title: To measure a child's exit code, suspend errexit for that command and capture $?; never let a predictable failure kill your loop
summary: Under set -e a command that returns nonzero is meant to abort. But when you must keep running and just record why a child stopped, you have to turn errexit off for exactly that child and read $? immediately. The same discipline applies to commands whose nonzero return is a normal 'found nothing' signal rather than a fault.
technique: Run the volatile step with errexit disabled, wait the pid, capture its code, then restore normal flow; clean incidental side processes with an explicit `|| true` instead of a bare semicolon so the earlier code is preserved. Reserve a small set of nonzero codes to carry a diagnosis rather than flattening everything into one exit 1.
evidence_note: queuebash.sh:27618-27625 uses `set +e; wait "$cmd_pid"; rc="$?"` to run a job worker and keep going, then maps overflow into a sentinel like rc=96; it also uses `... || true` to tidy loggers without swallowing the worker code. queue-vcs-probe:165 uses `... || true` on a probe that must not abort.
invariants: When you must survive a failing child, scope errexit off for that invocation and read its code into $? / a named rc at once.
Keep real stages under set -e; do not globally disable it to dodge a bug.
Let a 'nothing found / not a repo / no such row' state be a distinct first-class result, not a fake success or a crash.
Treat reserved nonzero codes as carrying meaning (log cap, caps violated, usage, missing tool) rather than a single generic failure.
